surfaces.part: flat ground at the foot of the stairs

answer.evidence: The stair block (rows 0-31) repeats a light snow tread of 4 rows and a white front-edge line (rows 4/12, 20, 28). Each is followed by a dark 3-row riser (rows 5-7, 13-15, 21-23, 29-31). That gives four treads, each about 5 rows tall, with a 3-row vertical riser in front of it, so the top surface and front face are both drawn. The cliff walls at the left and right edges are narrow vertical strips with no receding side plane. Rows 32-47 are flat ground texture and do not affect the stair reading.

styleAnswer.evidence: The measured facts are mixed. The candidate has 8 visible tones per tile against 3 for grass and 7 for paving, and 0% neutral dark edge pixels, so its outlines are tinted rather than near-black. By eye it is still shallow. The stair treads are white and pale blue-grey with only about 3 lightness steps and no per-step grain, chips or snow speckle. The beige landing at the bottom is a large flat fill with no dots or grain. 26% of the candidate is near-flat, while both references are 0%. It has only 13 distinct colours in total, and the paving reference shows far more stone-by-stone shading. Next to the references it reads as flatter and more sticker-like, so it fails.

surfaces.part: flat ground at the foot of the stairs

answer.evidence: Rows 0-31 hold the stair run. Each step has a light snow tread of 4 rows, topped by a white front-edge line (rows 12, 20, 28), and a dark riser of 3 rows below it (rows 13-15, 21-23, 29-31). The tread, edge line and riser pattern repeats, so each step shows both a top surface and a south face. The darker rows under each edge line act as eave shadow. Rows 32-47 are flat brown ground with no step structure. The width is a constant 32, so no side face is drawn.

styleAnswer.evidence: The candidate reaches 8 visible tones per tile against 3 for the grass and 7 for the paving, so tone count alone is not a problem. The snow has no clumps or crystal dots, and the references show per-stone or per-tuft variation across the whole tile. The ramps are shallow, about 4 steps against 5-6 in the references. Next to the references the piece looks flatter and more graphic, so it fails.

answer.evidence: Rows 0-31 are a flight of steps. surfaces.part: ground at the foot of the stairs

answer.evidence: Four stacked snow treads (rows 8-11, 16-19, 24-27, plus the top landing in rows 0-4) are each 4 rows tall. A 1-row white front-edge line (rows 12, 20, 28) closes each tread. Below each edge line are 3 rows of dark riser and shadow (rows 13-15, 21-23, 29-31) that form the vertical face. This alternation of tread, edge line and riser is the 3/4 view of steps. The ground in rows 32-47 is a flat tile. No side face is drawn.

styleAnswer.evidence: The measured facts look acceptable on the surface: 8 visible tones per tile against 3 for grass and 7 for paving, and 0% neutral dark edge pixels, so the outline is tinted. By eye, though, the piece is shallow. The snow steps are built from about 4 tones, which is a few blue-grey and white bands with no grain, speckle or per-step shading. The beige-pink landing at the bottom is a large flat block with no soil grain or variation. Near-flat coverage is 26%, while both references are at 0%. The whole palette is only 13 colours, against 80 for the grass reference. Next to the textured grass and the stone-by-stone paving, it reads as a clean, thin, sticker-like graphic. When in doubt, fail.
